title: 2nd Grade Addition Word Problems: 3 Story Types + Free Quiz
meta_title: 2nd Grade Addition Word Problems + Free Quiz
meta_desc: Teach 2nd grade addition word problems the clear way: combine, increase and compare stories with 2-digit numbers, a solve method and a free quiz.
excerpt: A Grade 2 child can add 28 and 15 on paper, then freeze the moment those numbers hide inside a story about mangoes. The fix is teaching the three addition story types, not more sums.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Give a Grade 2 child ‘28 + 15’ in a column and most will carry the ten and write 43 without blinking. Now wrap the same numbers in a sentence — ‘Riya picked 28 mangoes on Monday and 15 on Tuesday, how many in all?’ — and watch the hesitation. The maths did not get harder. The reading did. That gap is exactly what 2nd grade addition word problems are meant to close, and it is the single biggest reason a confident calculator still loses marks on a test.

In my experience the trick is not more sums. It is teaching children to recognise the shape of the story. Almost every addition word problem at this level is one of three types, and once a seven-year-old can name the type, choosing to add stops being a guess.

The three addition story types

Grade 2 word problems that call for addition come in three flavours. Say the type out loud with your child until they can spot it themselves.

1. Combine (two groups joined)

Two separate amounts are put together and you want the total. ‘There are 34 boys and 29 girls in Class 2. How many children in all?’ Nothing changes over time — two groups simply sit side by side and you join them: 34 + 29 = 63.

2. Increase (something grows)

You start with an amount and more is added. ‘A shopkeeper had 46 pens, then bought 27 more.’ This is the story type where time moves forward, which is why it trips up children who were told addition means ‘putting two piles together’. Here there is one pile that gets bigger: 46 + 27 = 73.

3. Compare (how many altogether)

Two amounts are named and the question asks for their combined value. ‘Aarav has 18 stickers and Meera has 25. How many do they have together?’ It looks like a comparison because two people are set against each other, but the word together gives it away — you add: 18 + 25 = 43. Watch this one closely, because the same setup with ‘how many more’ would flip it into subtraction.

A four-step method that works every time

Once the type is clear, the solving follows a fixed routine. I teach it as four steps and insist the child does all four, not just the middle two.

  • Read it twice. Once to hear the story, once to catch the numbers. Rushing the read causes more wrong answers than weak arithmetic ever does.
  • Underline the numbers and the question. Circle 28 and 15, then underline ‘how many in all’. Now the page is doing half the thinking.
  • Name the type and write the sum. ‘Combine, so I add: 28 + 15.’ Set it out in columns if regrouping is needed.
  • Answer in words with the unit. Not ‘43’ but ‘43 mangoes’. The unit forces a sanity check — 43 mangoes makes sense; 43 would be marked wrong on most Indian school papers anyway.

Clue words help — but do not trust them blindly

Words like in all, altogether, total, both and sum usually signal addition. They are a useful first hint. But here is the caveat I wish more worksheets printed: clue words lie often enough to be dangerous. ‘Ravi had 50 rupees and spent 20. How much is left?’ has no addition word at all, and ‘How many more does Sara need?’ contains ‘more’ yet means subtraction. Teach clue words as a nudge, never as a rule. The story type is the real guide.

Story typeWhat is happeningExampleSum
CombineTwo groups joined34 boys, 29 girls in all34 + 29 = 63
IncreaseAn amount grows46 pens, buys 27 more46 + 27 = 73
Compare (together)Two amounts totalled18 and 25 stickers together18 + 25 = 43

Regrouping hides inside the story

The reason Grade 2 addition word problems feel harder than Grade 1 is the two-digit numbers, and with them, carrying. ‘A basket has 57 apples and 28 are added.’ The ones column is 7 + 8 = 15, so you write 5 and carry 1 ten; the tens become 1 + 5 + 2 = 8, giving 85. A child who is shaky on regrouping will read the story fine and still land on 75. If word problems keep going wrong by exactly ten, the culprit is the carry, not the comprehension — drill the column method separately for a few days, then return to the stories.

Easing into two-step problems

By the end of Grade 2 many children meet their first two-step problem, and addition is the gentlest place to start. ‘A shop sold 23 laddoos in the morning, 19 at noon and 15 in the evening. How many in all?’ That is two additions stacked: 23 + 19 = 42, then 42 + 15 = 57. The lesson is to solve one step, write the part-answer, then use it. Children who try to hold both sums in their head stumble; children who write 42 down do not. Keep these to three friendly numbers at first — the goal is the habit of stepwise working, not big arithmetic.

Try the quiz, then the printable practice

Below is a free 8-question quiz built from these exact story types — combine, increase and compare — with 2-digit numbers and honest explanations for each answer. Let your child work through it, then talk over anything they miss. When they are ready for longer written practice, the printable worksheet linked at the end gives graded mixed word problems with a full answer key you can print as often as you like.

quiz.title: 2nd Grade Addition Word Problems Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight story problems covering combine, increase and compare with 2-digit numbers. Read each twice, pick an answer, then press Check my score.

questions.q: Riya picked 28 mangoes on Monday and 15 on Tuesday. How many in all?
questions.explanation: Combine story: 28 + 15. Ones 8 + 5 = 13, write 3 carry 1; tens 1 + 2 + 1 = 4. That gives 43 mangoes.

questions.q: A shopkeeper had 46 pens and bought 27 more. How many pens now?
questions.explanation: Increase story: 46 + 27. Ones 6 + 7 = 13, write 3 carry 1; tens 1 + 4 + 2 = 7. That is 73 pens.

questions.q: Aarav has 18 stickers and Meera has 25. How many do they have together?
questions.explanation: The word 'together' means add: 18 + 25 = 43 stickers. 'Together' points to addition; 'how many more' would mean subtraction.

questions.q: Which word usually signals that you should add?
questions.explanation: 'Altogether' (like 'in all' and 'total') usually signals addition. 'Left', 'fewer' and 'difference' point to subtraction.

questions.q: Class 2 has 34 boys and 29 girls. How many children in all?
questions.explanation: Combine story: 34 + 29. Ones 4 + 9 = 13, write 3 carry 1; tens 1 + 3 + 2 = 6. That is 63 children.

questions.q: A basket had 57 apples and 28 were added. How many apples now?
questions.explanation: Increase story: 57 + 28. Ones 7 + 8 = 15, write 5 carry 1; tens 1 + 5 + 2 = 8. If you got 75, you forgot the carry.

questions.q: A shop sold 23 laddoos in the morning, 19 at noon and 15 in the evening. How many in all?
questions.explanation: Two-step: first 23 + 19 = 42, then 42 + 15 = 57. Write the part-answer 42 down before adding the last number.

questions.q: Which of these problems needs addition, not subtraction?
options: Ravi had 50 rupees and spent 20; how much is left?
Sara has 12 pens; how many more to reach 20?
A jug had 40 ml; 15 ml was poured out; how much remains?
A box has 36 balls and 24 more are put in; how many now?
questions.explanation: Putting 24 more into the box grows the amount, so you add: 36 + 24 = 60. The other three take an amount away.

faq.q: How do I know when a Grade 2 word problem needs addition?
faq.a: Name the story shape first. If two groups are being joined, or an amount is growing, or two amounts are being totalled 'together', it is addition. Clue words like 'in all' and 'altogether' help, but the story type is the real test.

faq.q: Why can my child add on paper but not in a word problem?
faq.a: The arithmetic is fine; the reading is the hurdle. Word problems ask a child to turn a sentence into a sum, which is a separate skill. Practising the read-underline-name-solve routine builds it quickly.

faq.q: Are clue words like 'total' and 'more' reliable?
faq.a: Only as a hint. 'More' can mean addition ('27 more pens') or subtraction ('how many more to reach 20'). Teach clue words as a nudge and let the story type make the final call.

faq.q: When should a 2nd grader start two-step word problems?
faq.a: Usually late in Grade 2, once single-step addition and regrouping are secure. Start with three friendly numbers to add, and insist the child writes the part-answer before the final step.
